Live from NPR News, I'm Joel Snyder, a five-ton stockpile of degraded bomb-making
material at a facility in southeast Iowa is on track to be detonated later this morning.
The U.S. Army says it's taking numerous precautions, as Iowa Public Radio's Eliza Billingham reports.
The explosive lead azide is already in earthen bunkers. The Army previously said it would wet
the land with misters to prevent as much dust as possible from being released from the explosion.
Colonel Aaron Teller, who's in charge of the detonation's mitigation efforts,
added that his team is also planning to flood the area with two feet of particle-trapping foam
to further contain dust spread. This is an unprecedented amount of both protection works
and mitigation measures. Our goal is to get to zero, zero release of lead particulate.
The Army released worst-case scenario maps of the furthest as might spread. The Army says
it will update those maps frequently. For NPR News, I'm Eliza Billingham in Iowa City.
Kilmara Brego Garcia has self-deported. The Salvadoran immigrant became a symbol of
the Trump administration's immigration crackdown after he was wrongfully deported
and then brought back to the U.S. Here's NPR's Juliana Kim.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen wrote on X that "Kilmara is traveling to a country of his choice,
a free man, unharmed, and with dignity." The Democrat has played a leading role in
championing a Brego Garcia's case since last year, when the man who had been living in Maryland was
deported to El Salvador by mistake. The details of a Brego Garcia's voluntary departure are unclear,
but it comes after months of sparring with the Trump administration.
A Brego Garcia said he was willing to move to Costa Rica, but the federal government did not
support those plans and instead sought to deport him to a country in Africa. Juliana Kim, NPR News.
Now overseas to Saudi Arabia, where officials say 11 people were wounded Tuesday in an attack on a
high-rise tower in the capital's financial district. NPR's Aya Batrawi reports on the
second Houthi attack on the public investment fund tower in less than a week.
Saudi Arabia's emergency rescue service posted a photo online showing several floors of the
skyscraper damaged. It says 11 people were wounded in this latest attack, among them Saudis,
Egyptians, Indians, and Nepalese. Saudi Arabia blamed the attack on the Iran-backed Houthis,
who are targeting Saudi oil sites, airports, and Riyadh's financial district with missiles and
drones. The Houthis say they also struck Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in Rastanura in
the east, sparking fires there. The kingdom has yet to comment. Most international flights
to Riyadh have been suspended since mid-October, and high-profile events have been cancelled
because of these attacks. Saudi airstrikes, meanwhile, are targeting the Houthis across Yemen
daily. Aya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai. This is NPR. A deadly plane crash Tuesday off the coast of
Mississippi. The U.S. Coast Guard says six people, including two young boys, have been found dead
after their Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island.
The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board are expected to investigate.
More than half a dozen Colorado ski areas are set to open this holiday week, with several delaying
their first day of operation due to warm weather. Beaver Creek, the latest to push back its opening
day until after Thanksgiving, Colorado Public Radio's Stena Sieg reports. Beaver Creek Resort
says the delay is despite the foot of new snow that fell last week. It simply isn't cold enough
yet at the ski area's lowest elevations to operate. Beaver Creek joined several other resorts that
have announced they'll open later than originally projected. Last winter, many resorts opened behind
schedule due to warm, dry weather, creating the worst snowpack in decades. This winter, resort
owners and skiers hope the climate phenomenon known as El Nino will deliver lots of snow,
but meteorologists say there is no guarantee. For NPR News, I'm Stena Sieg in Grand Junction, Colorado.
Pakistan's first astronaut in orbit, now the first foreign astronaut aboard China's space station.
China state broadcaster Cishan Ali and two Chinese astronauts entered the station today,
having docked their Xinzhou-24 spacecraft about three and a half hours after launch,
the joint flight part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in 2025. This is NPR News.
